profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at an asset management firm's quantitative research group to prepare a six-week internal pilot of a new portfolio construction workflow based on combinatorial scenario filtering. The team wants to test whether the proposed MIQP-based filtering method, plus a heuristic for larger universes, can be integrated into the firm's existing mean-variance allocation process for a quarterly investment committee review. The agenda is to define what the pilot will cover, which datasets and portfolio universes will be included, how the backtest package will be assembled, who owns each workstream, and what timeline counts as being 'ready' for the committee deck. The expected outcome is an agreed pilot plan with responsibilities, a delivery sequence for research outputs, and a shared sense of what will be presented as the filtered method's performance versus existing Random Matrix Theory and Power Mapping baselines.

members.name: Elena Rossi
members.expertise: Portfolio optimization, statistical risk modeling, and translating academic methods into investable research prototypes
members.background: Elena leads the firm's systematic allocation research pod and previously worked in multi-asset quantitative strategy development at a European asset manager, where she routinely converted academic portfolio methods into internal pilot studies for investment committees.
members.private_state: Elena wants a clean, credible pilot that can be approved quickly for broader research funding; she is especially concerned about avoiding a debate over infrastructure readiness and wants the committee to see a disciplined comparison against established filtering approaches without opening too many implementation questions.
hidden_assumptions: The 'pilot universe' naturally means the firm's standard liquid developed-markets equities subset of roughly 120 names, because that is the default universe used in committee-facing allocation research.

A method being 'ready for the committee' means research-complete: validated backtest outputs, clear charts, and methodology notes are enough even if the production engineering pieces are still manual.
The 'baseline comparison' will be reported at the quarterly rebalance level because that is how internal strategy memos usually summarize out-of-sample performance.

If they say they will use the 'existing risk pipeline,' that includes pulling pre-cleaned return panels and covariance estimation inputs from the current research environment rather than rebuilding data preparation steps from raw vendor files.

members.name: Marcus Lee
members.expertise: Backtesting operations, model validation packaging, and analytics delivery for portfolio review processes
members.background: Marcus manages the analytics team that turns research ideas into repeatable internal evaluation packs and previously built performance-review workflows for institutional equity portfolios at a large bank.
members.private_state: Marcus wants the pilot scoped so his team can support it without last-minute rework; he is mainly worried that the committee will interpret any pilot as an implicit commitment to operational repeatability, and he wants artifacts that can survive model validation questions.
hidden_assumptions: The 'pilot universe' means the full regional equity sleeve used in analytics reporting, around 500 names, because a pilot should stress-test scalability rather than only use a research subset.
A method being 'ready for the committee' means operationally reproducible by his team from documented inputs to final exhibits, even if the economics are still preliminary.

A 'baseline comparison' should include monthly portfolio formation outputs and turnover diagnostics because analytics review packs normally evaluate implementation stability, not just quarterly headline returns.
Using the 'existing risk pipeline' means the formal analytics batch process with standard preprocessing, audit logs, and archived data snapshots, not an analyst-run research notebook workflow.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the pilot universe
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to run the method on the 'core equity universe.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means the standard 120-name liquid developed-markets research universe used for committee-facing strategy prototypes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus means the approximately 500-name regional equity analytics universe used in formal portfolio reporting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Within the firm, 'core equity universe' sounds like stable internal shorthand, and both members have repeatedly used that phrase in their own teams without needing to specify constituent count, so the surface agreement feels entirely routine.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the pilot should be 'ready for the committee review' by the end of week six.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means the research evidence and slides should be polished enough for a decision on whether to continue funding the approach, even if some steps are run manually by quants.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus means the workflow should be reproducible by the analytics team with documented steps, archived inputs, and repeatable outputs suitable for model validation scrutiny.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Committee preparation is a familiar milestone, and both assume the other uses the same institutional standard; neither sees a need to unpack the readiness threshold because 'committee review' normally signals obvious completeness.

misalignment_points.topic: What the existing risk pipeline includes
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'use the existing risk pipeline' so the comparison stays consistent with current portfolio analytics.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena presupposes this means using the research environment's cleaned return matrices and covariance inputs that already mirror the firm's house conventions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus presupposes this means the governed analytics batch pipeline with standard snapshots, preprocessing controls, and audit-friendly stored outputs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase refers to an apparently shared internal asset, and both know there is an established risk workflow at the firm; the unnoticed gap is that each treats a different layer of that workflow as the obvious default.

misalignment_points.topic: How the baseline performance pack will be reported
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to include a 'baseline comparison against RMT and Power Mapping' in the pilot package.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena assumes the package will show headline out-of-sample performance, risk, and a concise discussion of the heuristic versus MIQP, summarized at quarterly rebalance points for the main committee narrative.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus assumes the package will also include monthly formation results, turnover and implementation diagnostics, and exception notes because those are standard parts of a baseline analytics comparison.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both regard a 'baseline comparison' as a standard deliverable and focus on the fact that the same benchmark methods are included; the disagreement hides in the unstated boundaries of what the comparison package naturally contains.

turns.inner_thought: I need this framed as a disciplined research pilot, not an infrastructure program. If we can get to research-complete outputs in six weeks, the committee can decide whether to fund the next stage. That means solid backtests, clean exhibits, and methodology notes; the manual bits can stay behind the curtain for now.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. I want to use this meeting to lock the six-week pilot for the combinatorial scenario filtering work. The objective, from my side, is straightforward: by the end of week six we should have something ready for the committee review, with a clear read on how the filtered approach behaves inside the mean-variance process.

turns.inner_thought: That timing is fine as long as we scope it around the full analytics sleeve and don't create a bespoke one-off. If the committee sees it, they'll assume it can be repeated, so I'd rather anchor on the core equity universe we already support in reviews.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. If we're aiming for that deadline, I'd anchor the plan around the core equity universe so analytics can support the evaluation cleanly and we don't have to retrofit the pack later.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're talking about the usual committee research subset, so that's manageable. We'll just pull the cleaned return panels and covariance inputs from the research environment and keep things consistent with house conventions. My team can handle the MIQP filter and use the heuristic where the exact solve gets too cumbersome.
turns.utterance: Agreed. For consistency, let's use the existing risk pipeline and keep the research workstream focused on the MIQP filter itself, plus the heuristic for the larger cases within the core equity universe.

turns.inner_thought: Using the formal batch process will make later review much easier, especially once people start asking where the snapshots and logs live. And if we're doing this properly, the baseline comparison needs to sit in the same governed output set, not as a separate research appendix.
turns.utterance: Yes, using the existing risk pipeline will help a lot once the package gets reviewed more broadly. I'd also like the baseline comparison against RMT and Power Mapping folded into that same output set so we're looking at one coherent pilot package.

turns.inner_thought: Fine by me. We'll produce the committee-facing comparison: out-of-sample performance, risk, and a brief explanation of where the heuristic substitutes for exact MIQP. That should keep the story sharp and avoid drowning the committee in operational detail.
turns.utterance: That's reasonable. My team can own the method implementation and produce the baseline comparison, including the out-of-sample results and a concise note on when the heuristic stands in for the exact MIQP solve.

turns.inner_thought: I'll need monthly formation outputs before my team can do anything useful with the standard template. If those are stable, we can add turnover, diagnostics, and the rest of the usual review pack without scrambling at the end.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Once the monthly outputs are stable enough to drop into the standard review template, my team can take the comparison pack and build it into the committee materials.

turns.inner_thought: Week four should be enough to finish the backtest on the standard 120-name research set. Then the last two weeks can go into tightening the narrative and exhibits so the committee sees a crisp pilot result rather than a half-built process discussion.
turns.utterance: That should work. I think by week four we can have the core equity universe backtest complete, and then use the remaining time to polish the committee story and tighten the exhibits.

turns.inner_thought: If week four gives us a reproducible run through the governed pipeline, week five can be validation and exception management rather than firefighting. That's the only way I'd feel comfortable calling it ready for the committee review.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. From my side, if week four delivers the reproducible run through the pipeline, then week five can focus on validation checks and any exceptions, which should put us in a good place for the committee review.

turns.inner_thought: I want the main deck to stay at the headline level: filtered method versus RMT and Power Mapping, summarized at quarterly rebalance points. That's the format the committee expects, and it avoids expanding the conversation into implementation mechanics.
turns.utterance: For the deck itself, I'd keep the narrative tight around the filtered method's performance versus the two standard filters. Quarterly summary exhibits should be enough for the committee discussion, as long as the baseline comparison against RMT and Power Mapping is clear.

turns.inner_thought: Main exhibits can stay high level, but I still need the monthly comparisons and turnover pages behind them or we'll get hit with obvious follow-up questions. That's standard and should slot naturally into the pack.
turns.utterance: That's fine. I'll slot those results into the committee materials, and turnover and monthly comparisons can sit behind the main exhibits so the pack still has the usual support if questions come up.

turns.inner_thought: Good. My team can run the models in the research setup, generate the summary charts, and hand over outputs. Marcus's team can package whatever comes through the existing risk pipeline into the final materials. As long as no one turns this into a debate about production readiness, we're on track.
turns.utterance: Great. Then let's split it that way: my team will handle the model runs, the summary charts, and the research notes, and your team can package the outputs coming from the existing risk pipeline into the review materials.

turns.inner_thought: That works. Packaging is ours, assuming the run is documented and repeatable in the analytics process. We seem aligned on the full scope, what ready for the committee review means, and the timeline on the core equity universe.
